soil-water-269.title: Badlands, where clay and rare storms carve bare ground
soil-water-269.text: Some landscapes hold up to 464 kilometres of channel in a single square kilometre. These are badlands: dry terrain where soft sedimentary rocks and clay-rich soils are eroded into steep, bare ground with almost no loose cover. They form where an impermeable but easily eroded surface, sparse plants and rare heavy rains meet. Runoff cannot soak into the clay, so it cuts dense webs of gullies. Badlands National Park erodes at roughly 25 millimetres a year, helped by erodible bentonite clay. Too much grazing or poor farming can create them too, as at Ontario's Cheltenham Badlands.

soil-water-273.title: Clocking how fast a landscape wears down
soil-water-273.text: A landscape's lowering is slow enough to be quoted in centimetres per 1000 years. The commonest method starts at a river gauging station. Its suspended, bed and dissolved loads are converted to a volume and divided by the watershed area upstream. Stream load can vary fivefold between successive years, and the method assumes uniform erosion. Cosmogenic isotopes, mostly 10Be and 26Al, offer a check: their concentration in sediment leaving a basin falls as erosion speeds up. The stream power law, E = KA^m S^n, ties erosion rate to erodibility, drainage area and channel gradient.

soil-water-283.title: The Shields parameter: when a grain starts to move
soil-water-283.text: Albert F. Shields gave engineers a single number for the moment a sediment bed starts to move. The Shields parameter is a dimensionless shear stress, θ = τ / ((ρs − ρ) g D). Here τ is the shear stress, ρs and ρ the densities of sediment and fluid, and D the grain diameter. In effect it compares the fluid's push on a particle with the particle's weight. Motion starts at the critical Shields number. Shear stress belongs to the current, critical shear stress to the sediment. The Shields diagram is considered more precise than {{ref:soil-water-250}} for estimating suspended load.

soil-water-271.title: Corrasion, rock scoured by what water carries
soil-water-271.text: Running water alone barely scratches rock; the grit it carries does the cutting. Corrasion is mechanical erosion of the land by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement. On a river or sea bed, moving particles strike and grind the rock, and the wear they leave is called abrasion. Corrosion is different: the chemical, dissolving action of water on soluble rock. Lateral corrasion widens a river by cutting sideways, while vertical corrasion deepens its valley.

soil-water-279.title: Causes and triggers: why slopes fail when they do
soil-water-279.text: A landslide can have many causes but only one trigger. Causes are the conditions that make a slope vulnerable; the trigger is the single event that finally sets it moving. The trigger is easy to spot afterward but hard to predict. Causes may be geological, such as weathered or jointed material, or morphological, such as slope angle, erosion and vegetation change. Others are physical or human, such as forest clearing, excavation and mining. Following Terzaghi, internal causes weaken a material's resistance to shear stress, while external causes raise the stress. Earthquakes trigger slides by shaking and by raising pore water pressure, and the shaking is strongest at slope crests.

soil-water-280.title: Rain, the trigger behind most landslides
soil-water-280.text: Of 210 damaging landslides worldwide in the year to September 2003, over 90% followed heavy rain. Rain raises {{ref:soil-phys-098}}, which buoys slope material and weakens its grip, while groundwater flow can push downslope. Water also turns old debris into debris flows, removes suction in silty soils, undercuts a slope's toe and opens soil pipes. In 1980 Caine proposed a worldwide threshold, I = 14.82 D^-0.39, with rain intensity in mm per hour and duration in hours. It applies from 10 minutes to 10 days.

soil-water-292.title: Sediment yield, a river's report on its watershed
soil-water-292.text: A river's muddy load is a running report on the land upstream. Sediment yield is the amount of sediment per unit area of a watershed that a river removes over a period of time. It shows ecologists the health of river ecosystems, the pace of erosion and the effects of people. When late 19th-century Polish farmers switched from grains to potatoes, yields rose so much that meandering rivers became braided. Dams, reservoirs and detention basins upstream reduce it. Watershed runs of {{ref:soil-water-111}} predict it for whole catchments.

soil-water-289.title: Soil piping, erosion that tunnels underground
soil-water-289.text: Some erosion happens out of sight. Soil piping is the gradual internal erosion of soil by seeping water, which carves underground pipes that drain water downstream. Badlands sometimes hold whole systems of pipes, joints and caverns. Concentrated seepage out of a stream bank hollows out a pipe, and collapsing pipes in dispersive soils help form gullies. During rain, piping can loosen earth on slopes. In an earthen dam, a small leak can grow into a channel that leads to failure.

soil-water-290.title: Filter strips, grass that catches runoff
soil-water-290.text: A band of grass at a field's edge can catch what rain washes off the field. A vegetative filter strip is a strip of grass or other permanent plants that shields streamside land from runoff carrying sediment, pest-killing chemicals, pathogens and nutrients. Strips work best when other conservation practices steer water toward them. Once mainly agricultural, they are now common in towns. They are not the same as a {{ref:soil-water-109}}. The mapping tool AgBufferBuilder designs them by mapping where uneven runoff flows.

soil-water-295.title: Geomorphology, the science of how landforms evolve
soil-water-295.text: Every hill, valley and beach is the running total of what has been added and what has been taken away. Geomorphology studies the origin and evolution of landforms shaped by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near Earth's surface. Water, wind, ice, fire and life all act on the land, along with the chemical reactions that form soils. Landforms change through the balance of additive processes, uplift and deposition, against subtractive ones, subsidence and erosion. The work falls into three stages: producing regolith by weathering and erosion, transporting it and depositing it. Soil scientists usually study weathering, but geomorphologists need it because it supplies the material that moves. Soil, regolith and rock travel downslope by creep, slides, flows, topples and falls, while burrowing animals and falling trees set some hillslope rates. Soil geomorphologists read soil profiles and chemistry to learn a landscape's history. The field pays its way in landslide prediction, river control, stream restoration and coastal protection.

soil-water-293.title: Alluvial fans, cones of sediment at canyon mouths
soil-water-293.text: Los Angeles and Salt Lake City sit on alluvial fans. An alluvial fan is, a cone-shaped spread of sediment that fans out from a concentrated source, such as a narrow canyon opening onto a plain. Flow leaving a confined channel spreads out and drops its load. They range from less than 1 square kilometre to almost 20,000, with slopes of 1.5 to 25 degrees that are steepest near the apex, the fan's tip. Their sediments are coarse and poorly sorted, coarsest at the apex and finer toward the edge. Debris flows, stream flow or hyperconcentrated flows carrying 20% to 45% sediment feed them. Blocked channels periodically jump to new courses, so only part of a fan is active. Bypassed lobes undergo soil formation or erosion, and over 1,000 to 10,000 years may gain desert varnish or a soil profile from windblown dust. Neighboring fans can merge into a continuous apron called a bajada. Their coarse beds are major aquifers in many regions. A channel shift on the Kosi River fan caused catastrophic flooding in 2008.

soil-water-294.title: Slope aspect: which way a hillside faces
soil-water-294.text: Two sides of the same hill can grow different soils. Slope aspect, also called exposure, is the compass direction a land surface faces. With slope grade, it describes the surface gradient, and its effects on a slope's physical and living features are called the slope effect. In the Northern Hemisphere, north-facing slopes are often shaded. South-facing slopes receive more solar radiation per unit area, so they are generally warmer and drier, with more evapotranspiration. Soil follows. A steep equator-facing slope holds about as much organic matter as level ground lower down, while a pole-facing slope resembles level soils higher up. Outside the tropics, slopes facing the early-afternoon sun usually have the least soil moisture and organic matter in a locale. Wind matters too. Windward soils tend to be shallower with more developed subsoils, while leeward soils collect more windblown particles. Aspect is one way topography shapes soil, as {{ref:soil-form-045}} describes.

soil-form-128.title: How hillslopes change shape over time
soil-form-128.text: For much of the 20th century, the shape of a slope was the central question of geomorphology. Hillslope evolution is the change over time in the erosion rates, erosion styles and shape of hill and mountain slopes. Three models competed until the 1950s. In William Morris Davis's slope decline, slope angles fall gradually as stream incision slows and slopes fill with fine regolith from weathering. In Walther Penck's slope replacement, tied to slowing denudation, the lowest part of the slope flattens first and the flattening spreads upward and backward. Flattening always runs from the bottom up. The third model, parallel slope retreat, needs constant rock strength and steady removal of debris such as talus from the slope's base. That is rare, except where a hard cap rock such as basalt overlies softer rock. Lester King championed parallel scarp retreat as globally dominant and saw slope decline as a special case in very weak rocks. He tied smooth convex-concave slopes to grass carpets that slowed surface wash, so creep did relatively more of the work. Colin Crick coined the term unequal activity: slopes in one area do not all develop at once, and with little river erosion they may be effectively stagnant. Modern work holds that slopes evolve in far more complex ways than any of the classical models imply.

soil-water-297.title: Hydrosere: how a pond becomes a wood
soil-water-297.text: Given centuries or millennia, a pond can turn into woodland. That plant succession, from open fresh water to land, is called a hydrosere. At first, sand and clay washed in from the catchment drive the change. Dead plankton decay into humus, which mixes with inwashed silt and clay into soil, and the pond grows shallower. Reed rhizomes knit the mud, and their tough litter builds reed peat. Sedge peat eventually rises above the water, so the soil is no longer waterlogged. Researchers still debate whether dry woodland is always the final stage or whether a bog can be a stable end point.

soil-water-296.title: Pedotope: all the soils of a place together
soil-water-296.text: A pedotope is the total soil part of the non-living matrix of an ecotope, the living and non-living whole of one location. It is not one kind of soil, nor even the dominant kind. It is all the soils of every variety present at that location, taken together. It is a term from {{ref:soil-found-095}}, the science of soils in their natural setting.

soil-form-129.title: Modeling the soil that slides down a slope
soil-form-129.text: W.E.H. Culling borrowed Fourier's heat equation to describe soil creeping downhill. Hillslope sediment flux models describe how much sediment moves on a slope at a given time, rather than how its shape changes. Culling wrote the flux as q = −K∇z, with K a rate constant and ∇z the slope gradient. This linear law works on gentle slopes but fails on steep ones. A nonlinear version adds a critical gradient, Sc. As the gradient nears it, erosion soars, perhaps representing landslides. Steep slope angles barely change even when erosion rises greatly, so steep topography cannot reveal erosion rates.

soil-form-130.title: Rounded soil-covered hills and the balance they hold
soil-form-130.text: Smooth, rounded hills draped in soil were long read as landscapes in balance. The idea goes back to William Morris Davis in 1892 and Grove Karl Gilbert in 1909. Such convex hills were taken to reflect a steady state between soil production and erosion. Yet soil depth on them can vary considerably, because bedrock weathers into soil at random. Formation rates may differ greatly even across a landscape in equilibrium. Models suggest broad, gentle hilltops in periglacial settings take millions of years to form. Tors often crown such hills, hinting that the original landscape was steeper.
